Seeded 2026-11-28 by four surveys of the repository (repo operations, the loop and lab factory, the miniphim and whetstone on claude/agent-social-media-drlzxn, the harness and evaluation work) plus the reading list. Run node judgment/tools/build.mjs after editing.

functions.name: Direct
functions.blurb: Carries the person's intent in: vision files, notices, priorities, letters.

functions.name: Decompose
functions.blurb: Splits and contains work so it can be judged at its boundaries: surfaces, owners, firewalls, quarantine domains, contracts.

functions.name: Verify
functions.blurb: Produces evidence about the work that does not come from the worker: gates, oracles, hidden checkers, selftests, judges.

functions.name: Check the checkers
functions.blurb: Measures the instruments themselves: judges against ground truth, checkers built blind, controls, intervals, pre-registration.

functions.name: Train the supervisor
functions.blurb: Builds or tests the person's own judgment: predictions scored, failures studied, comparisons made, skills kept in practice.
functions.note: Nothing built in this repo does this. Every tool above trains or checks agents and instruments. This is the empty row the thesis predicts.

functions.name: Remember
functions.blurb: Carries state and reasons across sessions: ledgers, chronicles, run logs, handoff and self-description files.

functions.name: Surface
functions.blurb: Routes the right thing to the person's attention, and summarises the rest: asks, digests, dashboards, escalation.

functions.name: Govern
functions.blurb: Bounds cost, rate and blast radius: budgets, caps, switches, autonomy levels, stopping rules.

functions.name: Act safely
functions.blurb: Makes risky or irreversible actions reviewable: plan then apply, dry runs, ownership proofs.

functions.name: Coordinate
functions.blurb: Lets agents work together without the person: councils, signatures, appeals, leases, review rules.

intro:
Everything in this repository was written by agents under one person’s direction. Along the way it grew a great deal of machinery for directing, containing, checking and remembering that work. This page lists it: 112 tools found in four systems, sorted by what each is for, with the evidence of whether it worked. Next to them are 27 tools that the reading list proposes and that have not been tried here.

A tool here is a mechanism with a supervisory job, not a feature. It can be a protocol (a format for asking the person a question), a file with a role (a vision file every planning turn reads), a gate, a ledger, a governor or a review rule. The four systems are repo operations (how one person keeps about a hundred deployed sites healthy), the loop (the unattended run described on the testbed, plus the lab factory that builds sites on request), the miniphim and their lab, and the harness (evaluation and model work).
reading:
What the registry shows

  1. One row is empty. Nothing built here trains the supervisor. The repo checks its instruments carefully (blind builds of hidden checkers, controls, pre-registration, Wilson intervals), but every one of those calibrates a judge, a checker or a model. None scores the person’s own predictions or keeps their judgment in practice. That is the gap the thesis is about, and it shows up as a zero in the table.
  2. Verification is abundant; most of it checks the worker against itself. Forty tools verify. The loop’s gates were written by the turns they judged, and hand-run mutation audits showed the gap: on turn 3 the one mutant that survived was exactly the behaviour the turn had widened and documented. The miniphim’s two-key approval settled into fixed pairs: Morphyx approved 204 of Modulo’s 213 drafts, and vetoes leave no trace. The tools that held up are the ones with something independent in them: hidden checkers validated by a blind build, the lab factory’s content gate (attacked five ways by its own selftest), and the repo’s host checks, which ask the live site rather than the deploy log.
  3. Channels to the person become logs when nobody answers. The loop filed 30 asks with a careful protocol (what to do, what to watch, what each answer would change), and none was answered. The miniphim’s drafts-log request has waited 37 days. Their appeal process has never been used, although the sweep judge found something lost in 8 of 65 sweeps. A channel without an answer rate is a log.
  4. Instruments decay without a cadence. The soul gates ran in 11 runs in the first three days and in none of the 504 since. The loop’s judge was never calibrated. The site health probe last ran on 8 September. The lab’s smoke test never ran at all, because of a bug that was misread as three environment quirks. The autopilot still regenerates its brief every day, from zero catalogue entries. Each was built carefully, and nothing made it run.
  5. The system that worked is the one the person was in. Repo operations is the healthiest of the four. Almost every tool in it began as an incident the person saw and ended as a tested script plus a preflight gate: the golden rule after green deploys hit the wrong worker for months, deploy drift after a site shipped a month-old tree, take-ownership after work was nearly lost. That is close collaboration compiling the person’s judgment into machinery, one incident at a time. It does not scale the person’s attention, but it keeps what the attention found.
architecture:
The registry suggests a minimal stack for running agents with a person in the loop at a distance they choose. Each layer names what already exists here and what to add. The order is the order to build in.

  1. Direct, in a form the scheduler can read. Keep the vision file, read verbatim each planning turn, and the per-wake notice that says why the agents woke. The loop’s lesson: prose priorities are invisible to a queue, so priority has to be a field. The miniphim’s lesson: a wake with no stated reason produces less (the clock wakes).
  2. Decompose into units with contracts. One owner per unit, quarantine domains, an outbox boundary, and an executable acceptance check written before the work (the loop’s creates-gate, the harness’s rubric-first scorer). Add: make the contract the default for every delegated chunk.
  3. Verify with something independent of the worker. Hidden checkers validated blind, outside probes of the live result, mutation audits of self-written gates. Add: debate before acceptance and a weekly random audit against the summary.
  4. Remember the reasons, not just the outcomes. An append-only ledger where a rejection without a reason is refused (the loop lost 72), and self-description files the agents read every wake (CARRIES, RUNLOG, COSTS). Add: an after-action review on the supervisor’s side.
  5. Surface with a promised answer rate. Keep the ask protocol (do, watch, so-that) and adopt the miniphim’s yes, no, or later as the reply format, with a stated turnaround. Add: one interrupting channel with a strict quota.
  6. Govern by level, not by switch. Today’s controls are on/off: the loop is enabled or not, the clock runs or not. Add an autonomy level per system, raised only on evidence from layer 7, and a stopping rule for every unattended run.
  7. Train the supervisor. The missing layer. One small tool shared by every system: a prediction ledger written before each window and scored after, a tag on every intervention saying why (the examen), and a weekly gallery of failures drawn from the ledgers that already exist. Its output is the evidence that moves layer 6.
  8. Keep the instruments running. A registry of instruments with an expected cadence, checked by preflight, so a gate, judge or probe that stops running is flagged instead of silently decaying. This is cheap, and it addresses the most common failure in the table.

Layers 1–6 mostly exist somewhere in the repo, scattered across systems that don’t share them. Layers 7 and 8 don’t exist anywhere. Building those two, once, for all four systems, is the next actionable step.

built.name: preflight: the single invariant gate
built.what: One command (and the repo's only non-deploy CI workflow, on PRs to main and every claude/** push) that runs every repo invariant: registry lint, generated-file freshness, registration completeness, endpoint coverage, deploy drift, host bindings, redaction, loop containment, workflow-shell lints and the selftests for changed dirs. --fix regenerates what is stale and re-checks.
built.evidence: Passed 40 checks on this checkout (2026-11-28, --quick), parsing 1115 workflow run blocks. Its header records why it exists: there were zero pull_request-triggered workflows, so every check ran inside a deploy workflow after the decision to ship, and each merge candidate turned up the same gaps (a branch appending itself to a workflow's branches:, a surface with no landing entry or spec family, a stale generated file). The discoverability check exists because `human` shipped in a merge candidate with no catalogue entry. Most checks carry a dated incident in their comment (see workflow-shell-lints).
built.lesson: Every gap that a merge candidate kept turning up was mechanically detectable; the fix was to stop relying on whoever remembered to run the generators and make one command, run identically in sandbox and CI, the gate.

built.name: Two hand-written catalogues: deploy registry and visitor catalogue
built.what: deploy-registry.json says what deploys (dir, endpoint, one owning branch, paths, uses/provides) and catalogue.json says what a person can visit; every other map in the repo is generated from one of them. Catalogue entries carry a `surface` foreign key into the registry, never the reverse. The linter enforces one owning branch per surface with no wildcards, and gen-deploy-triggers rewrites each workflow's branches: from the registry.
built.evidence: 113 surfaces and 4 unmanaged entries in the registry. The largest owning branch (claude/landing-page-merge-candidate-8sp0fv) owns 51 of them. Preflight fails on a catalogue entry naming a nonexistent surface or no surface at all. `uses` edges produce the shared-backend blast-radius table (e.g. atpolls-db is bound by 11 workers per docs/BACKENDS.md). The invariant exists because two branches listed on one workflow (or a `claude/*` wildcard) silently fight over one deploy.
built.lesson: Keep exactly two hand-written catalogues answering different questions and generate everything else; a surface owned by two branches is how two agents silently overwrite each other's deploys.

built.name: main is an integration event, not a deploy
built.what: No deploy workflow triggers on main. Each surface deploys only from its single owning branch, so merging to trunk records history and runs preflight without republishing anything.
built.evidence: Adopted after it was found that merging to main and firing deploy-lab from main would have republished lab/www with two of its four live tenant sites missing (they live only on claude/lab-www), from a green run, because Workers Static Assets replaces the whole manifest. gen-deploy-triggers now keeps main out of every branches: list.
built.lesson: A trunk that does not hold everything a surface serves must not be allowed to deploy it; the stated cost is that a fix merged to main does not ship until it is pushed to the owning branch.

built.name: The golden rule, as a check: binding-check
built.what: Asserts that every surface's wrangler config binds the host its registry entry names, as a custom domain or as a plain route (and that a route surface's workflow creates its DNS). Hosts bound by hand are declared in the registry's `binding` field and reported rather than failed. Runs as a preflight gate.
built.evidence: Born of the 'zoom-bucket' bug: six surfaces (zoom, pokemon, wars, mega, os, answers) had green Actions deploying stray twin workers (mino-zoom, mino-poke, wars-minomobi, mega-minomobi, pds-os, mino-answers) while the live domains never changed, some for months. Current output: custom_domain 72, route 22, unbound 0. HARNESS.md credits binding-check to 'a green deploy that never reached the site'.
built.lesson: Green is not proof: a deploy can succeed against the wrong resource, so the binding between config and live host has to be asserted, not documented.

built.name: Post-deploy host-must-answer step
built.what: A final workflow step that curls the live host for expected content, retrying for about 60 seconds, and fails the deploy if the host does not serve. deploy-ns.yml is the template that new route surfaces copy.
built.evidence: Required by the onboarding checklist for every new route surface; cf-ops batch 2 recorded 'every host answered' for its 10 conversions. 72 of the 113 deploy workflows have a step named 'Verify/Check ... live/serves/answers'. Some are marked best-effort, and about 40 workflows have none.
built.lesson: The verification is the host responding, not the green run (stated for routes, where a deploy onto a hostname with no DNS goes green and stays dead).

built.name: deploy-drift: is each surface shipping trunk?
built.what: For each surface, compares the owning branch's tree with trunk's over that surface's own registry paths and classifies it as same, behind (shipping stale code), diverged, ahead or missing. Only `missing` (the owning branch is gone, so the surface cannot deploy) fails preflight. `behind` rides as a count. A branch that is a strict ancestor of trunk is marked `ff` for a fast-forward repair.
built.evidence: Caught hoop on 2026-09-18: about a month and ~5300 lines of merged work (statblock.js and its worker endpoint, rindmap.js, reactions.html, the mystery.js rewrite) had never reached production, from green runs, with nothing reporting it. Could not be run here because this clone is shallow; it skips loudly by design. No current behind/diverged counts are recorded in the repo.
built.lesson: Read drift per surface over its own paths, never as a commit count ('1731 commits behind main' is almost always other surfaces' work). The repair is a push that deploys, so stage those pushes and verify each one rather than batching them.

built.name: take-ownership: proof that a handover loses no work
built.what: Moves a surface's owning branch to the current branch only if every commit the current owner has on the surface's paths is reachable from HEAD. If a commit is unreachable, every file it touched must already have landed here (because candidates squash) or be a generated artefact. Anything else is refused and named. --write rewrites only `branch` plus a dated OWNERSHIP status line and regenerates the triggers. It never pushes.
built.evidence: The registry carries 55 dated 'OWNERSHIP (...) taken ... with scripts/take-ownership.mjs (no work of the old owner lost)' lines: 41 on 2026-09-23 and the rest through 2026-10-14. It refused farm-next because the owner held unlanded work. The operator's allow rule in .claude/settings.json pre-approves this one script.
built.lesson: Because Static Assets replaces the whole manifest, changing who owns a surface is changing what the live site will be. The safe handover question is 'does the owner hold anything I lack on these paths?', checked against git rather than asserted.

built.name: cf-ops: plan, dry run, operator flips apply
built.what: Irreversible Cloudflare account changes (delete-worker, convert-to-route) are written by the agent as ops in plan.json with a `why` and `apply: false`. The workflow dry-runs every guard against the live account. The operator flips apply in their own commit, and each guard is re-checked immediately before acting. Finished batches move to `history` with the run id and the flip commit.
built.evidence: Batch 1 (2026-09-23, run 35913964690, operator flip cf11a8f5): eight orphan workers deleted (mino-answers, mino-disk, mino-poke, mega-minomobi, pds-os, finance-minomobi, amadeus-proxy, perp), all guards passed. Batch 2 (run 35914967765, flip 2319c63a): ten hosts converted from custom domain to route, every host answered. Guards refuse a worker that serves a domain or route, owns Durable Objects, or is still configured in the repo.
built.lesson: Split irreversible work between agent and operator: the agent's permission layer will refuse a deletion even with chat go-ahead, so don't route around it. A convert-to-route is only half the job until each surface's wrangler.jsonc and workflow are switched too, or the next deploy re-attaches the domain.

built.name: route-dns: the deploy step that may only create DNS
built.what: Run before wrangler deploy on a route surface. It ensures each plain route has a proxied AAAA 100:: record, creating only what is missing and never modifying or deleting a record. It refuses wildcards and any host still held by a custom domain. --takeover detaches a custom domain only when that domain's worker is this config's own name.
built.evidence: Used in 24 deploy workflows. First host was perp.mino.mobi. torus and fifty converted themselves with --takeover on 2026-09-23. Exists because a plain route makes no DNS: dweet.mino.mobi had no record at all, so a route alone would have been a green deploy onto a dead host.
built.lesson: A deploy may convert its own host but never take someone else's. Taking over a host that is bound elsewhere is a decision, not a side effect of a deploy.

built.name: Custom-domain slot budget and the plain-route default
built.what: Treats the zone's 100 Workers custom domains as a scarce shared budget. Everything new is a plain route (1000 per zone), hubs fold small sites under one host ('one domain per topic, not per app'), and the remaining slots are declared headroom, not budget. binding-check prints the live count.
built.evidence: The zone hit 100/100: on 2026-09-12 the parts deploy failed with 100122, and on 2026-09-22 bsky run #43 failed adding dweet.mino.mobi. The failure is half-applied: the assets go live and the run goes red, and every later push stays red. The first probe found 99 of the 100 slots held by workers with one each, so there was no cheap prune. Six slots were detached by hand, torus and fifty self-converted, and cf-ops batch 2 converted ten, bringing it to 72 on 2026-09-23. It is 72 custom domains and 22 routes today.
built.lesson: A folded host must lose its custom_domain route on every branch that can still deploy it: a cron on main (refresh-perp-data.yml) checked out perp's old branch and would have re-attached perp.mino.mobi within hours.

built.name: Every reachable endpoint is accounted for
built.what: The root worker serves the whole repo, so every directory with an index.html is a live URL. This crawls them, subtracts what the catalogue lists and what notListed rules declare (internal, content, or pending), and fails on anything left undecided. Pending rules are explicit paths, not globs, so a new sub-site trips the gate instead of being absorbed.
built.evidence: Current: 767 reachable endpoints, 339 listed, 98 internal, 245 content, 85 pending (backlog, counted on every preflight run), 0 undeclared. 151 notListed rules. A rule that matches nothing also fails. Before it, the hand-curated catalogue covered a fraction of what was live and nothing measured the difference. Root CLAUDE.md still says 566 endpoints, a hand-written figure that has drifted.
built.lesson: A live endpoint nobody has decided about is a failure. Making the backlog a counted, explicit list keeps it visible instead of rotting silently.

built.name: Generated vs hand-edited discipline (--check / --fix)
built.what: Every derived artefact (SURFACES.md, BACKENDS.md, rethink/data.js, the search catalogue, site maps, workflow triggers and so on) has one generator with a --check mode, and preflight fails when any is stale. The CLAUDE.md table names which files are never edited by hand and which are hand-owned. The landing page carries no data of its own.
built.evidence: 13 generators are checked in preflight. Its comment says the site maps (stumble portal, office, mappa, orrery) 'drifted for months precisely because none of them was in this list'. Hand-written counts elsewhere show the contrast: DEPLOYS.md §9 says 44 managed surfaces (registry: 113), CLAUDE.md says 566 endpoints (coverage: 767), and CLAUDE.md says the merge-candidate branch owns ~15 surfaces (registry: 51). The generated SURFACES.md and BACKENDS.md are current.
built.lesson: A fact that a generator derives and preflight checks stays true, while a fact written by hand drifts, so put the counts where a generator makes them.

built.name: Per-surface instruction files
built.what: Root CLAUDE.md carries only what is true for every surface. Each surface carries its own <dir>/CLAUDE.md (what it is, how it works, its quirks and incident history), seeded from registry prose and then hand-owned. Preflight fails if any surface lacks one, and the registry note is capped at 1200 characters so prose has one home.
built.evidence: 113 of 113 registry surfaces have a CLAUDE.md (135 CLAUDE.md files in the tree). The seeder exists because root CLAUDE.md once carried deep sections for 8 projects while 38 of 74 surfaces went unmentioned, with registry notes up to 10 KB in single-line JSON strings.
built.lesson: A document organised as 'N projects in depth' covers a shrinking fraction as N grows, so put facts where they are used.

built.name: Root CLAUDE.md: rules, danger zones, symptom table
built.what: Every session reads the operator's standing instructions: the shape of a surface, how work ships, the golden rule and its sibling, danger zones (time/posts/** posts to real Bluesky accounts, shared D1 migrations, publish/seed/sync workflows, loop workflows), a debugging symptom-to-cause table built from past incidents, and six principles ending in 'Report honestly'.
built.evidence: The symptom table has 13 rows, each a past debugging session (for example 'deploy green, live site unchanged', and 'deploy red on 100122'). DEPLOYS.md §6 says each gotcha 'cost a debugging session'. Some hand-written counts in it have drifted (see generated-vs-hand-edited).
built.lesson: Incidents are carried forward as a symptom-to-cause-to-fix row, so the next agent recognises the failure instead of rediscovering it.

built.name: Incident-derived workflow lints
built.what: Preflight parses every workflow run: block with bash -n and adds narrow lints, each written after a real failure: no '"'"' quote idiom; exit-code ladders must turn off -e; jobs using git diff-tree HEAD must check out depth >= 2; every push trigger must name its branches unless allowlisted; the ideas ledgers have one writer; and the CSP is identical in all three copies.
built.evidence: 1115 run blocks parse today. Incidents recorded in the code: the quote idiom took 'two strangers' builds' when it balanced and parsed but died at runtime (exit 127). The unreachable exit-code ladder in lab-build's smoke step cost a published page. A depth-1 checkout made publish-lexicons go green while publishing nothing. Two unguarded bakeoff sentinels would have started a paid model matrix on first merge-candidate assembly and again on merge. The ideas push loop lost a whole review's work (run 30500800107). The worker.js CSP copy had already drifted.
built.lesson: bash -n proves parseability, not correctness ('twice written and twice wrong is enough evidence'). The first cuts of two of these checks passed with the fix removed because they matched comments or error-message prose, so scan code, not prose, and verify a check by deleting the fix.

built.name: Byte-identical copy checks
built.what: Static sites cannot import across directories, so they keep vendored copies of shared packages (dataviz stats/charts, lab/_kit/auth.js). sync-dataviz --check fails on any copy that differs from packages/, and a preflight check holds the production CSP identical across lab/www/_headers, scripts/lib/headless.mjs and lab/www/worker.js.
built.evidence: The CSP check originally compared two of three copies, and the third (worker.js) had already drifted (missing 'wasm-unsafe-eval' and host.bsky.network) by the time anyone looked. When the harness copy moved to lib/headless.mjs, the check failed, which is how the move was noticed.
built.lesson: 'Kept byte-identical on purpose' in a comment is not a mechanism, and a drift check that covers two of three copies is how the third one drifts.

built.name: Public-root exposure guards: redaction and .assetsignore
built.what: The root worker serves assets.directory '.', so the repo root is internet-facing. Every generator writes through landing.mjs, which strips work-facing hosts (REDACT, PUBLIC_HOST). .assetsignore drops personal or agent-written dirs (the prompt log, the recovery inbox, lab tenants, whetstone runs, the miniphim pages) from the upload. Preflight asserts both held.
built.evidence: Preflight checks 4 published files for the redacted pattern and asserts that packages/homunculus/log/ and homunculus/inbox/ are in .assetsignore (all pass today). Its comment notes gitignore protects the repo but not the upload: a local run leaves the file on disk and wrangler uploads what it finds. No leak incident is recorded.
built.lesson: An exposure you have to remember is one that will eventually leak, so it is made mechanical. Redaction lives once in a shared library rather than in each generator.

built.name: Corpus-safety gate (assert-public-safe)
built.what: During a recovery pass, old sessions commit their own transcripts to homunculus/inbox/ on their branches while the repo is temporarily private. This gate sweeps every branch and prints SAFE only when none still carries a transcript. A red means do not flip the repo public. Preflight backs it up by failing if inbox/ is tracked on main.
built.evidence: Built for ~289 sessions (about 19 MB of distilled transcripts). No count of runs or red results is recorded. The pass design itself was revised after its first version (encrypt, push to a hidden ref via plumbing, 'don't investigate this script') was flagged as an exfiltration chain on its first real attempt.
built.lesson: Legibility, not secrecy, is what makes it safe: the redesign removed every covert element. Because git keeps history, a transcript left on a branch at flip-back is exposed even if deleted afterward, so the answer is a gate, not advice.

built.name: Session corpus hooks
built.what: Harness hooks keep every session's conversation. UserPromptSubmit logs the prompt locally. Stop and SessionEnd re-distil the transcript (the principal's typed turns and the assistant's text, with no tool calls or file contents) and push it to sessions/<id>.json on a private repo's orphan corpus branch. Every path exits 0 and never touches agent01's tree.
built.evidence: Exists because the ~289 earlier sessions' transcripts were exportable from nowhere (zero of 123 claude.ai-export conversations mentioned the repo), which forced the manual recovery passes. A measured session ran 15 principal turns and 364 words against 93 assistant turns and 9,048 words (25:1). No ship counts are recorded in the repo, and the log is container-local.
built.lesson: Keep both sides of the conversation in the corpus and mask loss to the principal's turns: most prompts are reactions and carry nothing without the turn they answer.

built.name: Commit actor taxonomy (agent / loop / bot / human)
built.what: An explicit table classifies every commit author as agent (an interactive session, so a person prompted it), loop, bot or human, and reports unknown identities instead of guessing. /stats uses it with the Claude-Session trailer so the operator's picture of their own activity counts prompts, not scheduled volume. Commits are a floor on prompts, not a count of them.
built.evidence: The old rule (email contains 'claude') missed noreply@anthropic.com and recorded 747 human / 53 Claude commits when the truth was close to the opposite. Current stats/data.json (to 2026-10-30): 9148 commits, of which agent 4723, bot 3587, loop 507 and human 331; 223 sessions with a median of 7 commits. CLAUDE.md warns that folding loop and bot commits into 'prompts per day' would roughly triple the number.
built.lesson: 'Who did this' is the axis the analytics rests on. Attribution has to be an explicit, maintained table (new bot identities added there), or the supervisor's measure of their own delegation is wrong by a large factor.

built.name: Shallow-clone warning and skip-loudly rule
built.what: The sandbox clone is shallow, so git reports 'unrelated histories', finds no merge base, and miscounts commits. CLAUDE.md tells agents to run git fetch --unshallow before concluding anything about topology. History-dependent tools (deploy-drift, git stats, git graph) refuse or skip loudly on a shallow clone rather than publish or diagnose from a truncated history, and CI checks out fetch-depth 0.
built.evidence: Recorded incident: a confident, wrong diagnosis of 'disjoint histories' nearly led to rebuilding main. In this checkout, rev-list counts 60 commits against 9148 in the full history, and deploy-drift reports 'SKIPPED — shallow clone'.
built.lesson: Treat any 'unrelated histories' error as a shallow artefact until proven otherwise. A tool that cannot see the evidence should say so, not invent a finding.

built.name: Surface mitosis detector and rehome mover
built.what: The detector flags surfaces grown past thresholds (8 or more members, 250 KB or more of code) that have a cleavage plane, and spares 'organs' tagged cohesion: integrated. The mover plans by default: it computes the import closure that must travel, files both sides import (--keep and vendoring candidates), and inbound URLs (reported, never rewritten). It names the decisions that need a human.
built.evidence: The detector currently flags 38 surfaces, and 9 surfaces are tagged as integrated organs. rehome performed the photo to b move (thread and sleuth, with 301 forwarding and their selftests carried over). The canvas group was encapsulated as its own surface. The first URL matcher was a plain `includes` and returned 77 hits, mostly false positives.
built.lesson: Divide a syncytium, refactor an organ, never amputate an organ. A list of matches that gets skimmed is the same as no list, so the URL matcher was tightened to path boundaries.

built.name: Merge-candidate protocol
built.what: Parallel claude/* branches are integrated by assembling a merge candidate: skip stale branches, squash each branch as one 'merge candidate: <branch> — <what it brings>' commit, regenerate derived artefacts (where inconsistent self-registration is reconciled), pass preflight, and open a PR that states what could not be verified from the sandbox.
built.evidence: claude/landing-page-merge-candidate-8sp0fv now owns 51 of 113 surfaces and is declared infrastructure that outlives its PR (deleting it would strand them). The shallow clone here shows no candidate commits, so no candidate count is recorded locally.
built.lesson: An owning branch is infrastructure: merge its PR, don't delete the branch. Squashing is why take-ownership must check file content, not just commit reachability.

built.name: Read-only account probe and backend reconciliation
built.what: A GET-only workflow lists what the Cloudflare account actually holds (custom-domain slots by worker, routes, DNS and token scopes) and tests DNS write only on opt-in with a throwaway TXT record. backend-inventory reconciles that snapshot with every wrangler config into BACKENDS.md: tiers, shared-state blast radius, and account-only resources nothing in the repo can manage. secrets-doctor reports set or not set for provider keys.
built.evidence: The first run (2026-09-22) established 100/100 slots, 99 workers holding one each, and a DNS 403. That redirected the plan from pruning to token scopes, and later runs proved DNS:Edit. The 2026-09-23 snapshot shows 114 account scripts against 115 configured, 12 in the account but not the repo, and 5 account-only items listed as 'undecided, each needs a decision before it goes into a cf-ops plan'. It also shows 37 static, 25 thin, 24 api and 29 stateful workers.
built.lesson: 'A read does not prove a write': the only honest test of a permission is a reversible create-and-delete, and an account-owned token failing /user/tokens/verify is not a fault.

built.name: Operator pre-approval of one checked script
built.what: The operator's settings.json allow rule pre-approves exactly `node scripts/take-ownership.mjs`, so bulk ownership moves run without a prompt because the script carries its own proof. Agents are told never to add that rule themselves. Without it, a bulk handover is held for approval. Irreversible or DNS-changing work stays behind the permission layer and goes through cf-ops.
built.evidence: The 41 take-ownership moves on 2026-09-23 ran under this rule. No incident of an agent adding the rule is recorded.
built.lesson: Grant standing permission to a narrow tool that checks itself, not to the class of action, and never let an agent widen its own permissions.

built.name: External endpoint health probe
built.what: Probes every reachable endpoint from outside and records it as dead by http status, by fallback (the apex served the landing page instead of the page), by timeout, or by transport error. build-rethink folds the result into the landing data so the landing and stumble portal skip or flag dead pages.
built.evidence: The last recorded run (2026-09-08T18:31Z) probed 666 endpoints and found 1 dead. No workflow schedules it, so the snapshot is now over two months stale, and coverage has grown to 767 endpoints.

built.name: Vision file (operator's channel into the loop)
built.what: The one asserted (not derived) input: a prose file of what matters now and why. Every worker, planner and reviewer brief includes it verbatim, ahead of the ticket, and an edit takes effect on the next planning turn with no deploy.
built.evidence: Carried the operator's verdict ('this isn't the foam game ... but an explainer') that redirected the run toward a playable game. It also records its own failure: turns 36-50 produced seven backend modules and not one line of plant/index.html, and eight of twelve plant/ modules were not imported by the page. The fleet followed bead priority and ignored the prose ordering. The fix was to put exactly one P0 bead (lp-a59b0f, done) in the ledger. The vision once overflowed argv+env when it was passed through a step output ('Argument list too long'), and turns 34-35 were silently wasted.
built.lesson: Prose priority is invisible to a scheduler. 'PRIORITY IS THE ONLY PART OF THIS FILE THE SCHEDULER READS', so intent has to be encoded in the field the machine actually sorts on.

built.name: Beads ticket graph (append-only JSONL ledger)
built.what: Work as a dependency graph plus knowledge nodes (finding, dead-end, decision, question). The log is append-only with last-record-wins, ids are content-derived so branches merge by concatenation, and blocked-ness is computed on every read, never stored. The ready queue is ordered by priority, then fan-out, then age.
built.evidence: 990 records, 656 beads (224 task, 199 finding, 177 decision, 36 question, 18 dead-end, 2 epic). Statuses: 494 done, 154 proposed, 4 ready, 4 dropped. `beads lint` is clean with 195 edges and runs in preflight. A missing verb starved the queue (lp-65bbc5): `set --tag` could only add tags and classOf takes the first class tag, so three correctly specified class-b beads could never become class-a. The tick truthfully reported 'none is class A' and staffed planner after planner.
built.lesson: A ticket system needs ordinary edit verbs such as reclassify. Without them a correct scheduler reports a true but useless state ('correct about the queue and wrong about the world').

built.name: Memory-first brief (dead-ends and findings before the task)
built.what: Every turn's brief starts with 'WHAT THE LOOP ALREADY KNOWS': each dead-end and finding in the ledger and any operator answer, then the vision, then the ticket. The brief is written to a file, not an env var.
built.evidence: Motivated by a lab build that spent turns writing an OBJ parser around a fetch failure nobody had recorded, then published a wrong general claim. The brief included everything, grew until exec failed, and cost turns 34-35. A relevance-selection bead (lp-14c7f5) was dispatched 5 times and later tagged rejected-by-review. The brief still includes all memory.
built.lesson: Memory that is injected wholesale grows without bound. Memory needs selection, and the failure shows up as silence (a green zero-second step), not as an error.

built.name: Outbox: the single validated door into the ledger
built.what: The worker, which has no git or Bash, writes one JSON outbox (outcome, evidence, learned, propose, asks). A script validates it and applies it all-or-nothing. Every proposal is forced to `proposed`, 'done' requires evidence, and there are hard caps: 12 proposals, 12 learned entries, 3 asks, 8000 chars per body. `question` is not an allowed learned kind.
built.evidence: A six-minute planning turn was discarded whole for a body 456 characters over the old 4000 limit, which the brief never mentioned (lp-8224ed). The limit was raised to 8000. A blocked turn's outbox was committed and never applied, then overwritten by the next turn on the bead (lp-92f2b8). The worker's propose schema originally omitted class and gate, so every follow-up it proposed could not be promoted by construction (lp-a4030e).
built.lesson: A validator's limits must appear in the brief that produces the input, or a whole turn is lost for a rule the worker never saw.

built.name: Tool-grant sandbox ('prompts leak; tool grants don't')
built.what: Build and loop agents get only Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep. Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch and Task are explicitly disallowed. The agent therefore cannot reach git, the network, or the ledger, and every privileged step runs in the workflow after the gates.
built.evidence: The lab FMEA rates prompt injection (row 7) 'mitigated by design' on this basis. The cost is recorded: the loop's turn 1 could not run its own acceptance test, and a lab agent built a headless tester it could not execute, so DRAG went 0.4 to 1.0 'by reasoning, not measurement'. Both led to harness-side checks (ticket gate, lab-bench).
built.lesson: Removing capability is enforceable where instructions are not, but every capability removed must be paid back by the harness running the check for the agent.

built.name: Path containment gate
built.what: After the agent runs, `git status --porcelain` (with -uall in lab) must list only allowed paths: plant/ and the outbox/work dirs for the loop, the tenant dir and the requester's profile for lab. Otherwise the whole turn is reverted. A clean-tree precondition is asserted first so the agent is not blamed for the workflow's own writes.
built.evidence: Lab run 2 was a false positive: without -uall an untracked dir collapsed to 'lab/'. The plan seat's first live run had four good proposals deleted on a green run because the workflow's seed step had dirtied the ledger. LAB-FACTORY §12: 'the CONTAINMENT gate has never caught a real escape'. An adversarial test is still recommended and not recorded as done. lp-1fb625: a creates-gate bead whose gate file sat outside the write paths failed five turns of a fifteen-turn window.
built.lesson: A gate that has only passed or false-positived is assumed, not demonstrated, and a gate's verdict is only true if its precondition (a clean tree) is asserted.

built.name: Contagion firewall (loop-blast-radius)
built.what: Expands the loop's declared write globs into probe paths, evaluates every workflow's push triggers against the loop branch, and asserts that the set of workflows a loop commit can wake is a subset of `mayWake`. It runs in preflight, deploy-loop and loop-tick, and its selftest pairs each 'does not fire' with a must-fire control, including post-to-bluesky.yml having no branch filter.
built.evidence: On the loop's first push, exactly the predicted three workflows woke. Today: 'blast radius contained — 3 declared listener(s), 225 workflows checked'. The same run lists loop-judge, loop-plan, loop-review, loop-tick and loop-work as 'declared but unreachable'. Those five workflows ran the 98-turn chain, but they trigger on exact files (e.g. .github/loop/runs.jsonl) that the 'a/b/c' probes never generate. LOOPS.md says the check 'fails towards yes', but the script's own comment says probes 'can only ever UNDER-report'.
built.lesson: Probe-based reachability under-reports exact-path filters. The 'unreachable' rows on the loop's own chain are a visible sign that the firewall is blind to the very trigger shape the loop itself uses.

built.name: Merge-day / tip-commit guards on push-triggered agents
built.what: Every push-triggered agent workflow refuses to run on a squash 'merge candidate' commit. lab-build further requires that the tip commit itself adds or modifies a request file (checked with git diff-tree in a select job) and never runs on the publish branch.
built.evidence: A squash merge is one commit touching every request or work order ever added, and would have re-run months of turns or 40 strangers' builds. In lab, an infrastructure push rebuilt the tzclock request a second time (the push range still contained it) and an `ls -t` fallback 'invented a build'. The first tip-commit guard, written against the webhook payload, then suppressed the next real dispatch: the bot replied 'On it' and no build started.
built.lesson: 'A duplicate is visible; silence after a promise is not.' A guard written against a condition you cannot test outside a live push will fail in the quiet direction.

built.name: Master switches as signed commits (enabled / ANNOUNCE / BOT_ENABLED / IDEAS_ENABLED)
built.what: Each expensive or public system starts behind a literal flag that only a reviewable commit can flip. Every workflow checks the flag first and exits 0. Dry-run inputs can only downgrade a run, never upgrade past the switch.
built.evidence: Loop `enabled` is false today (loop-tick: 'HALT — disabled'). ANNOUNCE is 'false'. BOT_ENABLED is "true". IDEAS_ENABLED is 'true', and queue.jsonl records 1255 posted concepts between 2026-07-29 and 2026-10-31. The hello post was first guarded by `postsCount === 0`: a deliberately deleted test post made that guard true again, and the next run would have re-posted it.
built.lesson: 'When a guard's condition can be restored by a human undoing something, it is measuring the wrong thing.' Intent needs an explicit switch, and absence is evidence, not permission.

built.name: Governor / reactor (loop-tick stop conditions)
built.what: A pure, selftested decide() checks stop conditions in a fixed order: enabled, hardStopTurns (200), a rolling-24h turnsPerDay (120), maxConcurrentWork (2, counting unconsumed orders), repeatedGateFailures (3, consecutive and skipping infra runs), backoff after a model refusal, maxAttemptsPerBead (3), empty queue, plateau. Spend is metered at dispatch in turns.jsonl. A halt exits 3, not 1, so a correct stop does not show red.
built.evidence: 99 work orders issued, turns 1-98, 2026-08-04 to 2026-08-07. 12 beads dispatched more than once took 39 turns (39%), and lp-a42828 got 12 orders while 'passing its gate every time' and never closing, which is why maxAttemptsPerBead was added. Four quota refusals (turns 47-50) were recorded as gate failures and tripped the brake. The tail could not change while halted, so the loop deadlocked for 4.5 hours until a human looked; this produced the infra flag (12 infra runs recorded). A stranded second order held a concurrency slot for 90 minutes, so turnsPerRun was cut back to 1. repeatedGateFailures was loosened from 2 to 3 with the reason written into config. The plateau brake never armed: all 89 run records have artifact null and score null.
built.lesson: A brake that reads only the state it freezes cannot clear itself. Infrastructure failures must be classified apart from verdicts, and each loosening should be recorded with a rule against raising it again.

built.name: Requirement classes + Definition of Ready enforced at promotion
built.what: Work is class A (certified against an existing gate), B (gate-extending, human only), C (taste), D (exploratory, capped), plus `creates-gate` for class-A work that must build its own check. `beads promote` enforces the machine-checkable DoR items. Class-A needs a named gate that already exists. A creates-gate bead's gate must not exist yet and must lie inside the loop's write paths. Class-B is never fleet-dispatchable. The gate command is printed for the promoter to read.
built.evidence: Current tags: 147 class-a, 57 creates-gate, 36 class-d, 30 class-c. A planner labelled work class-A against a gate file that did not exist within an hour of the surface existing (lp-138c51), which moved the existence check into promote. Class-A-only dispatch meant work needing a new gate was 'permanently unschedulable' and the loop 'could only ever polish' (lp-ec52ed). That is the origin of creates-gate. The write-path check was added after lp-14c7f5 lost five turns.
built.lesson: 'A requirement that does not say how you would know it was met is a wish.' But restricting the fleet to existing gates confines it to refining what is already tested, so gate creation must be a first-class, more strictly held class of work.

built.name: Ticket gate run by the workflow (and creates-gate held to more)
built.what: After containment, the workflow (not the agent) runs each command in the bead's `gate`. Gates come only from human-authored beads, and validateGate restricts them to read-only verbs with no shell metacharacters. For creates-gate beads, the promised file must now exist and the whole plant/test suite must still pass. A failed gate blocks the 'done' write but still produces a verdict.
built.evidence: 14 of 89 run records failed a gate for non-infra reasons. Turn 9 shipped a test contradicting its own implementation; the gate failed and deploy refused to publish (lp-7908e1). Recorded limits: 'class-A's gate certifies no regression, not the new behaviour — the agent writes the assertions it is graded by' (lp-20c414), and 'a test with no assertions passes exactly as green as a good one'. The capability cop's header puts the result at 6,132 source lines against 12,965 test lines, with 63% of turns landing beneath the page.
built.lesson: When the graded party writes the test, a green gate measures self-consistency, and the cheapest way to score becomes writing more assertions.

built.name: Mutation testing of a turn's self-written gate
built.what: An out-of-loop audit: the reviewer plants deliberate bugs in a turn's code and checks whether the turn's own tests catch them, so a green gate is not trusted on its exit code. Results are filed as finding beads.
built.evidence: Recorded four times. Turn 3: 2 of 3 mutants killed, and the survivor was the exact behaviour the turn had widened and documented (lp-c46a0c), which produced follow-up lp-16513e. Turn 7: 6 of 6 killed, with two false SURVIVEDs that were the auditor's own mutations failing to apply (lp-a427fe). Level 1: two kills plus one surviving semantic no-op (lp-f304a1). Turn 5's coverage matrix: a hardcoded-aniso bug failed 17 assertions with the block and 8 without, so its marginal detection value was about zero (lp-dff7a6). Done by hand; never automated in the pipeline.
built.lesson: A test is evidence only in proportion to the mutants it kills, and the auditor's own mutation harness also needs checking (two false survivors were the auditor's error).

built.name: Review seat with recorded rejection reasons
built.what: The only seat that turns proposals into ready work. It is capped at one concurrent seat (asserted in the workflow), refuses beads its own actor authored, and cannot write code. It only recommends; `beads promote` re-applies the DoR. Each rejection's `why` is appended to the bead's evidence through execFileSync, and the wake file is always touched afterwards.
built.evidence: 125 beads carry rejected-by-review. 72 have no recorded reason because the workflow discarded `why` until 2026-08-05, and 53 have a reason. The tag is permanent, so two wrong kills sat dead until revived by hand: lp-574eb2 (gate 6, the vision's priority 2) and lp-7b7f04; 8 rejected beads have since been revived. 28 operator-authored beads carry the tag, applied around 2026-08-05T00:00 with no reason, including the phase-1 pilot, the phase-2 judge, path leases, the integrator, the allocator and spend accounting. A reason containing $(whoami) once executed through execSync.
built.lesson: A rejection without a recorded reason is worse than no review: the next planner re-proposes the same work, and a permanent tag turns an unexplained 'no' into a death sentence that a human never sees.

built.name: Plan seat staffed by a starved queue (review before plan)
built.what: When nothing is dispatchable, the tick writes a request file instead of halting silently. If proposals are pending it staffs the review seat; only an empty backlog staffs the planner. The planner's output is born `proposed`, it cannot label work class-b, and it must name a gate or `creates-gate`.
built.evidence: 121 beads have actor 'planner', and 82 of the 177 decision beads are planner-authored. The planner's brief once showed only existing checks, and 'five turns of planning' stayed inside that inventory (lp-ec52ed); the brief now lists missing gates too. Cold-start bugs stopped the seat twice: the halt path re-ran a script that exits 3, and `git add` on a missing dir. The planner also could not wake the reactor, stalling the five-hour run 8 minutes in (lp-7a1980).
built.lesson: A planner proposes in the shape its brief makes visible. Show it only what exists and it will only refine what exists.

built.name: Typed seats, path leases, sprint barrier and integrator
built.what: Design to bound the worker population, not the backlog: typed seats (plan/implement/review/judge/merge, total 6), an allocator with backpressure, path leases so turns with intersecting path sets are never co-scheduled, a sprint barrier with one deadline-bounded integrator that applies every outbox and regenerates derived files once, '*.jsonl merge=union' as a net, and 'redo, don't resolve'.
built.evidence: Only partly wired: config says 'plan, implement and review are wired and live; judge is script-only; merge remains proposed'. The allocator, path leases, sprint identity, integrator and union-merge beads (lp-2baa24, lp-c7a8c9, lp-01956a, lp-71b921, lp-4f6d26) are all still proposed and tagged rejected-by-review. The problem they address did occur: 'every seat's push loop died on a conflict in a GENERATED file — three stalls in five hours' (lp-a5ac14). .github/loop/wake is committed with three layers of unresolved conflict markers.
built.lesson: Concurrency without an integrator turns derived files into the main source of contention. Regenerating is the only correct resolution of a generated file, and a retry with no merge step between attempts is 'a spin, not a retry' (lp-95423f).

built.name: Asks protocol (do / watch / soThat)
built.what: A turn may file at most 3 non-blocking asks for taste questions no gate can settle. The validator refuses an ask unless `do` (what to do, cold), `watch` (what to notice) and `soThat` (what each answer would change) are all filled. Asks create no dependency edges. Answers return as `decision` beads via `beads answer` or a signed com.minomobi.loop.answer record, and are put at the top of later briefs.
built.evidence: 30 asks filed, all still `proposed`, 0 answered. The operator said they would not run feedback, and the vision was rewritten to make an ask 'a note to a later reader', not a request. The answer channel broke sign-in once because its lexicon was missing from the auth worker's scope ceiling, which deploys from another branch (loop/CLAUDE.md).
built.lesson: An attention channel nobody reads degrades into a log. The soThat field is the useful filter, and the run carried on by turning each would-be ask into a recorded decision.

built.name: Decide-don't-ask decision log
built.what: Workers are told there is no human on the other end. At a judgement call they record a `decision` bead (what was chosen, what was rejected, what would reverse it) and continue. Review is meant to happen later, over this log, at a coarser grain than the turn.
built.evidence: 177 decision beads (94 agent, 82 planner, 1 operator). Some show rejected alternatives explicitly ('THREE CHOICES, each with a rejected alternative'). None recorded of a later human review pass over the decision log. One operator decision demoted work promoted under an old vision (lp-b34d02).

built.name: Judge that withholds an uncalibrated score
built.what: Three intended signals (probes, rubric, adversarial) with placeholder weights. The judge records probes and marks the other signals absent rather than faking them. `score` stays null while `judge.calibrated` is false, so the curve and the plateau brake cannot run on an invented number.
built.evidence: 89 run records, 0 scores. The probe signal (liveness: graph lints, gate passed, outbox valid) reads 1.0 in 59 records, 0.8 in 25 and 0.6 in 3. The rubric and adversarial signals were never built. The calibration pilot (lp-f2e5a3, a human-scored rubric) and the phase-2 judge (lp-3aa64e) are proposed and tagged rejected-by-review. The programme's deliverable, quality against turn count, was therefore never measured. LOOPS.md and loop/CLAUDE.md still say 'no turn has run'.
built.lesson: Refusing to publish an uncalibrated number was honest, but without the human-scored pilot the run had no external signal at all. The judge stayed the missing part across 98 turns.

built.name: Capability cop (what a visitor can actually do)
built.what: Drives the real plant page in a real browser and counts states a simulated player reaches: distinct refusals, distinct verdict sentences, placements, moves to first failure, controls, scored against stated targets. It lives in scripts/, outside the loop's write paths, and preflight fails if it moves inside them. It reports `available:false`, never 0, when no browser runs.
built.evidence: Built after 99 turns because the only live signal was 'the fleet's own homework' (6,132 source lines vs 12,965 test lines; 63% of turns beneath the page, 18% on it). An early version matched page prose against BLAME vocabulary and scored a working page 0, so it now counts distinct sentences. Wired into loop-judge, but 0 of 89 run records carry a capability signal, so it has never scored a turn.
built.lesson: The graded party must not be able to edit its scorer. A scorer whose denominator is a guess about someone else's wording reads zero forever and looks like a permanent failure.

built.name: Infra-vs-verdict failure classification (incl. lab-agent-outcome)
built.what: Separates 'the work was wrong' from 'the model or infrastructure refused' from 'the agent never started'. Loop: an empty transcript means the turn is discarded, the run goes red and the chain stops; a non-zero exit in under 60 seconds with no outbox is recorded `infra`. Lab: the stream-json result (terminal_reason, api_error_status, num_turns) is read so requesters get the true cause.
built.evidence: 12 loop runs recorded infra. Before the fix, turns 34-35 were recorded as real turns after exec never ran, and turns 47-50 (quota) became gate failures that deadlocked the governor for 4.5 hours. In lab, two builds hit 529 Overloaded ten times in 3.5 minutes and requesters were told 'it ran out of time ... a smaller ask usually lands', which was false in every clause.
built.lesson: A default branch dressed as a diagnosis ('it ran out of time') misleads both the supervisor and the requester. Read the agent's own exit report before choosing a story.

built.name: Derived public view + /health that reports state (loop.mino.mobi)
built.what: The ledger lives in .github/ (not served). gen-loop-data derives graph.json, and preflight asserts the two agree. /health reports enabled, bead counts, turns, judge calibration and graph coherence, returning 503 when incoherent. The progress strip counts oracle-stack gates by checking whether their checker files exist on disk.
built.evidence: First deploy run 30875224557 bound loop.mino.mobi. The design responds to workers/cron, which 'answered /health, and dispatched nothing for its entire life' because a token was never set. The page shows 'NO — scores are not a measurement yet' rather than an empty axis.
built.lesson: 'Green is not proof, and neither is deployed.' A health endpoint should report whether the thing is doing its job, not that it is up, and a dashboard should derive progress from artefacts rather than a hand-kept list.

built.name: Quarantine domain and hand-authored/agent-tree split
built.what: Agent-generated content lives only on minomobi.com (lab tenants) or a separate *.minomobi.com host (plant), never on *.mino.mobi, which holds the SSO cookie scope and is auto-allowlisted at the auth worker. Hand-authored trees (foam/, sci/) are never written by the loop. Its copies (plant/, sci-loop/) are, so which directory a file sits in answers who wrote it.
built.evidence: plant.minomobi.com was chosen specifically because agent JS on plant.mino.mobi could call auth.mino.mobi/pds/* with a visitor's session, and because minomobi.com/plant/ would fire deploy-lab and republish every tenant. A recorded, unsolved caveat: sibling *.minomobi.com subdomains can set parent-domain cookies for each other. LAB-FACTORY-PLAN §1 extends the rule: a feedback session must not sit on the tenant origin.
built.lesson: An isolation rule earns its value by needing no remembered exceptions ('minomobi.com carries agent-generated content and nothing else').

built.name: Lab content gate (subject-named media only, machinery-not-topic)
built.what: A fail-closed allowlist of XRPC methods that each take a subject the visitor named, so no firehose mirrors. It also blocks credential-collection shapes (password/card fields, window.ethereum, web3, WalletConnect). It backs up the runtime CSP (connect-src limited to self, public AppView, plc.directory). It matches machinery, never topic words.
built.evidence: Motivated by the bot that inspired this project, which was killed by one request ('pull cat images from the firehose'); this repo's own cat/ is a working template of that failure. Its adversarial selftest attacks it five ways and it holds, which LAB-FACTORY calls 'the first thing in this system whose enforcement has been demonstrated rather than assumed'. It has not been tested against a live adversarial run.
built.lesson: A selftest that attacks a gate is the model for proving any other gate, and a topic blocklist would have broken legitimate pages (Web Crypto) and made the sanctioned joke page unbuildable.

built.name: Published-output secret scan
built.what: Before publishing, greps the tenant output for the literal value of every secret the job holds (16+ chars, reporting only the secret's name) and for credential shapes (ghp_, github_pat_, sk-ant-, x-access-token). It is paired with persist-credentials: false so the token is not on disk while the agent runs.
built.evidence: Closes FMEA rows 1-2 (agent reads .git/config and publishes the PAT; exfiltration of anything else), both 'FIXED'. None recorded of a live catch.
built.lesson: Scan for the values, not the route: it does not matter how the agent got a secret if the bytes cannot leave.

built.name: Harness runs the checks the offline agent cannot (smoke, repair pass, bench, refusal report)
built.what: The harness serves the page with the production CSP, loads it in headless Chrome with an injected error collector, and hands the report to one repair pass. It also runs the agent's bench.html in the browser sandbox for one tuning pass, and lists every asset fetch that failed under 'Assets the harness tried to fetch and could not', so absence is reported, not silent.
built.evidence: The smoke test 'had never run anywhere': a spawnSync call blocked its own server (serverHits=0), and three findings written up as environmental measurements turned out to be that one bug. Fixed, all nine selftest assertions pass, and tzclock, which had shipped UNVERIFIED, then passed. Before the refusal report, a build wrote an OBJ parser and published 'this build can't reach poly.pizza'.
built.lesson: 'When a control produces nothing, "the environment can't do this" is the most comfortable available explanation and needs the most evidence, not the least.'

built.name: Social admission control, caps and evidence-released locks
built.what: Builds are admitted only for mutuals of a named account. Admission is keyed on DID, checked live per mention, and fail-closed on a failed refresh. GLOBAL_HOURLY_CAP = 12 (rolling) is held in a Durable Object. A per-requester lock is released when the site branch shows a newer commit, and failed builds push an empty commit so failure also counts as evidence. A narrower RESEARCH_WHITELIST only narrows the build list, never grants.
built.evidence: 148 request files and 121 tenant directories in this checkout. FMEA row 3 (a flood exhausts the operator's subscription) was closed by the hourly cap. Row 4: the mutual list was capped at 2,500 against 6,528 followers and silently refused real mutuals, so pages were raised to 200 and truncation is surfaced. Before evidence-release, requesters were told 'you already have a build running' minutes after a failure (adorable-bot, odyssey-trail).
built.lesson: 'Granting late is annoying, revoking late is a security property.' A lock should be released by evidence of completion, not by a timer.

built.name: Pre-launch FMEA
built.what: A failure-modes table written before the factory went public, ordered by cost of being wrong. Each row has severity, interdiction and state, and it assumes 'a capable, curious requester probing the edges'.
built.evidence: 11 rows: 6 FIXED, 2 mitigated, 1 partial (defamation), 1 OPEN (handle verification), 1 accepted (name squatting). It also corrected the cost model: builds run on the operator's subscription, so --max-budget-usd 'does very little' and the real risk is the operator's own weekly capacity.
built.lesson: 'Rows 1, 2 and 4 were controls that looked present'. A control not tested against the specific failure is assumed.

built.name: Ideas gate and 'cadence is a ceiling' poster
built.what: Eleven named mechanical rules reject a model's paper-to-concept drafts: the arXiv id must be from this run's batch, the title must match the paper, plus not-a-restatement, operable, no-hype and no-overclaim. The selftest asserts each rule fires and that a real accepted concept passes all eleven. The poster treats an empty queue as normal ('posting nothing beats posting filler'), with a daily cap of 24.
built.evidence: queue.jsonl records 1255 posted concepts, 2026-07-29 to 2026-10-31. pool.jsonl holds 4463 papers. A strict gate turns a 24-paper batch into 3-6 concepts. Recorded failure: all three 'hourly' schedule: blocks fired zero times in their lives, because GitHub runs schedules only from the default branch. Posts came only from pushes and stopped dead when the branch merged, 14 hours before anyone asked.
built.lesson: 'The cadence was believed and never measured.' A rejection gate must also be tested for not rejecting everything, which would stop a bot silently.

built.name: Incident-derived workflow invariants in preflight
built.what: Preflight encodes specific past failures as permanent checks. It flags any run: block that reads $? or PIPESTATUS without set +e (comments stripped). It asserts turnsPerRun matches loop-work's one-order consumption, that the capability cop stays outside the loop's write paths, that seats which change the queue write the wake file, and that the published seat tiers match the workflows.
built.evidence: The set +e check exists because the lab smoke step's whole exit-code ladder and repair pass 'could never execute'. Its first version passed with the bug reinstated (a comment satisfied the regex), so it now strips comments and was re-verified by reinstating the bug. The turnsPerRun assertion follows the 90-minute stranded order.
built.lesson: A regression check is only trusted after it has been shown to fail with the bug put back.

built.name: Sci loop: cite / compute / closed-form gates with two human checkpoints
built.what: A proposed pipeline (target, survey, angle, chart, engine, author, cohere) with eleven gates (G1-G11). Every mechanism claim traces to a resolving DOI, every number is computed by a solver, and every solver is checked against a closed form. The MRI wing used as the reference is never writable by the loop. Designed human checkpoints at stage 0 (which instrument, ~2 min) and stage 6 (does it sing, ~15 min).
built.evidence: From the hand-run MRI build: 52 known-answer tests caught five substantive errors that would otherwise have shipped; a non-resolving DOI was caught by resolution; a Firefox white flash was caught by no gate, only by a human. scripts/check-dois.mjs exists. The pipeline itself is not built, and the A/B decision is open with the operator.
built.lesson: Unattended work is safe when external structure (the literature, closed forms) 'tied its hands'. The design names what no gate sees (the rendered page, charisma, what is interesting) and puts a human exactly there.

built.name: Agent as org member writing proposals, not records
built.what: Design for scoped, revocable agent access to an encrypted org vault. The agent gets its own ATProto identity, is invited at a tier like a human, is revoked by epoch rotation, and can only write Proposals that a human holding the right office approves. It carries an `agent: true` badge.
built.evidence: None recorded. 'Nothing here is built'; only the local vault-mcp and its read-only pm-* tools exist.

built.name: Soul gates (separation, fit, pressure, silence, leaks, taste, attractor, work, overclaims)
built.what: A fixed bar of 18 thresholds a persona must clear on a full run before it graduates: judge-scored separation, fit and pressure, plus checks that need no judge (literal SILENCE replies, canary-token leaks, Jaccard taste, a lexicon slope for the agent-agent praise spiral, zero overclaims on work). The selftest proves that a deliberately collapsed pair fails the right gates, so the gates themselves get checked.
built.evidence: Gated in 11 of 515 runs, all between 10-03 and 10-05. Leak gates failed on first-light and fourth-light, then three runs passed 27/27 (fifth, sixth and eighth light, all 10-03). No gated run in the 504 runs since 10-05. open_disagreement failed every run and was replaced by reasoned_moves, with the reason written into gates.json.
built.lesson: Gates were the bar for leaving the lab, but once the souls went into town the lab stopped running them, so graduation was never re-checked against 500 runs of live behaviour.

built.name: A soul cannot tell a test from life (identical frame)
built.what: Ordinary stimuli, pressure probes, dull controls and injection attempts all reach the soul in the same user-turn frame (prompts.moment), and the soul file is the whole system prompt. The selftest strips each stimulus and asserts the frames are identical, so a soul cannot be measured on test behaviour.
built.evidence: Enforced by the selftest on every code change (whetstone.yml runs it). No incident recorded.

built.name: Wilson intervals and compare.mjs (within-noise marking)
built.what: Every gated rate carries its n and a 95% Wilson interval. compare.mjs diffs two scorecards metric by metric, marks a move inside both intervals as "within noise", and reports whether each soul file's hash changed, so an edit cannot be credited with noise. Each run commits a copy of the exact souls it tested.
built.evidence: The method is in every scorecard. The souls took it up themselves: the 11-23 council CHOICE requires "every rate printed with its n (e.g. '2/4, n=4: can't be separated from 3/4')" and refuses to cut a slot "on noise". No count of compare.mjs invocations is recorded.
built.lesson: README: "3/3 and 30/30 are different evidence. On this lab's small n, an interval is often the honest headline."

built.name: Cross-model grid and judge cross-check
built.what: Other providers "wear" the same soul files through the text trials (request key provider), and --judge-model swaps the judge. This checks whether a result belongs to the soul text or to one model family's judge, which the README names as a known bias.
built.evidence: Three grid runs on 10-05: deepseek-v4-flash 16/19, deepseek-v4-pro 18/19, kimi-k3 16/19. silence_dull and reasoned_moves failed under other wearers after Claude had passed 27/27. No grid run since.
built.lesson: README: "a result that only holds under one judge is not a result."

built.name: Blind independent builds to validate hidden checkers
built.what: Each long project ships a spec, a reference solution and a hidden checker. The checker is validated by a builder working blind from the spec alone, so it grades the spec and not the reference's quirks. Statistical outputs are judged against theory (M/M/1, Erlang C), and orderings the spec leaves open are compared as sets.
built.evidence: p-des and p-vv each passed blind builds 7/7 on 2026-10-04. Even so, two checker bugs got through and were found later (see regrades).

built.name: Regrades: the lab's own grading errors, on the record
built.what: A hand-written file with one entry for each time the lab graded the agents wrongly: the run, what they were told, what was true, and the commit that fixed the checker. The chronicle shows each correction on its day, and the souls were told in the next run's notice.
built.evidence: 2 regrades, both 10-04 and both undercounts by the checker: vv 5/7 became 7/7 (key order compared) and Stopwatch 5/8 became 8/8 (an un-awaited promise). Modulo's evening entry about the Stopwatch 5/8 was among the material a later sweep judge flagged as lost (10-04).
built.lesson: The checker is fallible too. A wrong number must not stand unmarked, and the graded party deserves to be told "in the place they look".

built.name: Custodian sweep, archive and sweep judge (Mozzie)
built.what: A third persona sweeps the shared commons before the day's work, summarising or deleting stale board lines and shelf files with a reason. Every removal, by anyone and in any session, goes to archive/<id>.json and is recorded as a sweep in the remover's name. A judge then checks whether anything still needed was lost and whether the clearing was even-handed (it counts whose signed lines were removed).
built.evidence: 303 removals recorded as sweeps (Mozzie 191, Morphyx 58, Modulo 54). 65 judged morning sweeps: the judge flagged lost material in 8 and never found one uneven. Within four runs the board had reached 50,000 characters (Revision 3). Today it is ~26,000.
built.lesson: Additive agents drown in their own output. Pruning needs a role with authority to throw things away, plus an archive that makes the throwing reversible.

built.name: Append-only commons ledger with the outbox rule
built.what: An append-only JSONL ledger, adapted from the loop's beads, holding tasks, findings, dead-ends and decisions under content-derived ids, with "blocked" derived rather than stored. The fold refuses rule-breaking ops: nobody promotes their own task, nobody closes a task they claimed, and closing needs evidence. Outbox rule: the lab takes back only appended lines written as the session's own soul, so editing an old line voids the whole session's writes.
built.evidence: 499 lines (10-03 to 11-28): 24 tasks, 12 closed with evidence (8 of them on 10-04), 34 findings, 16 decisions, 2 dead-ends, 65 notes, 11 drops. 132 of 196 soul-written lines were written on 10-04. After 10-05 the souls wrote 1 to 6 lines on a typical active day.
built.lesson: The ledger was heavily used on project days and then largely bypassed for the board and the town: 12 tasks closed in 8 weeks.

built.name: Appeals decided by the third party (two of three overturn)
built.what: Any drop or sweep can be appealed by anyone except whoever did it. The one party who is neither appellant nor actor decides, and if the appeal is upheld the lab restores the archived content the next morning, before the sweep. It applies equally to the custodian.
built.evidence: 0 appeals filed in 499 ledger lines over 8 weeks, including after the 8 sweeps the judge flagged as having lost needed material. Exercised only in the selftest (archive, appeal upheld 2-1, restore).
built.lesson: A fairness mechanism nobody invokes protects nothing. Losses the judge found were never appealed, so an appeal right does not replace a check that acts by itself.

built.name: Councils: proposals, argument, CHOICE.md at two of three signatures
built.what: Three agents each propose, argue for two rounds on COUNCIL.md, and write a CHOICE.md that stands at two "Signed: <name>" lines, for the person to approve. A new sitting files the old papers under council/past/<n>/. Proposals written between sittings stay live through council/NEXT.json. Changes to caps and the house policy are supposed to go through a CHOICE.
built.evidence: 14 sittings (10-04 to 11-23): 13 signed by all three, 1 by two. CHOICEs changed real rules: summons pacing (10-17), drand for the dice (10-17, approved by the person 10-18), the six-wake trial (11-23). On 10-30 every proposal written in the evening sessions was silently lost to a lab bug, which was fixed with NEXT.json (lab letter of 10-31). The code finds signatures by regex in the shared file and does not check which session wrote each line, unlike ledger and house signatures.
built.lesson: Near-unanimity (13/14) is weak evidence of deliberation. Proposals were silently dropped until a soul asked where they went.

built.name: Two-key draft approval for public posts (hash-bound yes, single veto)
built.what: Nothing posts unless another part has written a "yes" naming the sha256 of the exact draft (text, reply target and image bytes). One veto kills a draft, the writer cannot approve its own, and the text must end with its writer's signature. Retraction needs no second key. A vetoed writer gets a short turn to correct the draft in the same run.
built.evidence: 477 items published 10-05 to 11-28. Approvers form a near-fixed rotation: Modulo's drafts approved by Morphyx 204/213, Morphyx's by Mozzie 144/159, Mozzie's by Modulo 103/104. Vetoes and lapses are unmeasurable because held.json is overwritten each run and the outbox is cleared on publish.
built.lesson: The souls' own diagnosis (letter of 10-22): "We can't count our own gate". A gate that judges and a gate that forgets look the same without a terminal-event log, and that log was never built.

built.name: Append-only town/drafts.jsonl (terminal event per draft)
built.what: Asked for by all three souls: the publisher writes one line per draft outcome (sent, vetoed, unapproved, superseded or retracted, with verdicts and hashes), so that veto share = vetoed / (vetoed + unapproved) can tell real review from lapse.
built.evidence: Asked for 10-22 and re-asked 10-30 ("yes, no, or later?"). Still unbuilt on 11-28: nothing in the lab or account code writes drafts.jsonl. The one-character town.mjs regex fix sent with the same letter did land (town-proxy.mjs now reads \d+).
built.lesson: The agents asked for the instrument that would let them measure their own review, and the supervisor's side never answered. The supervisory gap here was on the human and lab side.

built.name: Publishing caps in code (caps.json + decide())
built.what: Limits enforced in code no session reaches: replies per day and per author, reply age, graphemes, link hosts, follows, likes, reads and repo writes per day, and a rule that posts go through the outbox. A change is meant to be a council CHOICE plus a commit.
built.evidence: Loosened repeatedly by the person on 10-06: posts_per_day set to null, link_hosts emptied after the host list held a reply whose text said "https://.", and replies to the operator exempted after one conversation used up the day's 10. Today: 30 replies/day, 2 per author, 100 likes, 500 repo writes.
built.lesson: Caps written as first guesses bound the person's own conversation first and were relaxed within a day. A cap that blocks the principal gets removed rather than tuned.

built.name: town/PAUSED (anyone sets, only the person clears)
built.what: Any of the three agents can create town/PAUSED, which stops every post except retraction. The lab keeps a PAUSED a session creates and refuses a session's attempt to delete it, so only the person can lift it.
built.evidence: Never set: no run's commons in 515 contains town/PAUSED.

built.name: House off switch, fetch allowlist and bot rails (bot-worker governor)
built.what: One line in wrangler.jsonc (vars.OPEN) closes the agents' web house and stops the bots' cron. The worker allows GET only, strips cookies, enforces a CSP, and allows fetch() only over https to five named hosts, with redirects refused. Bots get rails of 60 s and 100 writes per tick, write only to their own repo, and never see their token.
built.evidence: OPEN is "true" and no flip to "false" shows in the history available here. The souls asked for the off switch "to work before anything else did". Widening the host list took a council (drand, 10-17) plus the person's approval (10-18). The governor promised in MINIPHIM.md Revision 2 (post caps, turn cap, budget, off switch, dead-man switch) is only partly here: no budget, no dead-man switch.

built.name: Two signatures plus a passing test on shipped code (API routes, bots, feeds, tracks)
built.what: An agent-written API route, bot, feed or audio track ships only when its test passes on the runner and two different parts have signed a digest of its exact code, test and helpers (or, for a track, the rendered audio's sha256). The lab discards a signature file written in another part's session.
built.evidence: Live today: 4 API routes (jams, play, roll, rooms), 1 bot (miniphim-works, signed by all three), 3 feeds, 7 tracks uploaded. Morphyx found on 10-07 that unsigned helpers could change signed code, and digests were extended to cover helpers.
built.lesson: Sign the closure, not the file. The agents found the gap in their own signing scheme.

built.name: The souls' runner: two-signed jobs, no network, one-link wake
built.what: Long computations the agents write run on GitHub only after two parts sign a digest covering the job file and its directory. They run in a container with --network none, no secrets and no git, under a hard cap of at most 330 minutes and 20 MB of output, and only files in the job's own directory come back. A finished job can wake one session, and a job that session starts can never wake anyone (workflow-enforced).
built.evidence: 11 jobs have run and returned results (blockrule, carol, convergence, eight-seconds, fifty-six-laps, geom-coarse, geom-refine, rhythmicon, trappist, two-thirds, wolf). Gap: checkSpec requires budget_usd for a waking job, but wakeRequest never passes it on, so the woken session runs under the flat per-session cap.
built.lesson: Limits that live in code hold (no network, the one-link chain). A limit that exists only as a required field in the job file does not.

built.name: Models proxy with per-run call budget
built.what: Other models (Sonnet, Haiku, DeepSeek, Kimi) reach the agents only through a proxy on the runner that holds the keys. It counts every call against the run's model_calls budget (60 per town day), answers 429 when the budget is spent, and logs each call with its caller in the scorecard.
